title: Filling the vacant Kitchener regional council seat
subtitle: Appointment over by-election, plus a closed session on tariffs, an individual, and Cambridge land matters.
overview: Regional Council chose to fill the vacant Regional Councillor – Kitchener seat by appointment rather than a by-election. It selected option 1A, which appoints the next-highest vote-getter from the 2022 municipal election {{vote:m1}}. That candidate has confirmed being eligible and willing to serve.

Councillors pointed to the precedent from the 2015 vacancy, the narrow gap in votes, and cost. The Kitchener clerk has estimated a by-election at about $800,000, and a by-election would also leave the seat empty for months. One councillor argued for an open application process instead, to reach a wider range of candidates.

Staff will confirm the candidate's qualifying address. The appointment by-law is expected at the special Council meeting on March 13, 2025, so the new councillor can start as soon as practical. Council also met in closed session on legal advice about an identifiable individual, tariffs, and land in Cambridge. The minutes record no decisions from it. Council then passed its confirming by-law and adjourned.

decisions.detail: Council selected option 1A, appointing the next candidate with the most votes in the 2022 election to the vacant Regional Councillor – Kitchener seat, rather than holding a by-election or taking applications {{vote:m1}}.

debate: Several councillors supported appointing the next-highest 2022 candidate, citing the 2015 precedent, the small gap behind the last elected Kitchener candidate, and respect for the voters' earlier choice.
Cost was a main argument against a by-election. Councillors cited an estimated $800,000 and said it would leave the seat vacant until about June, so close to the next election.
One councillor preferred an application and interview process. They said the community has changed in over two years and that an open call could draw more diverse candidates.

The same councillor raised concern that the candidate is employed by an area municipality. Staff said the Municipal Act does not bar this, and the candidate indicated a voluntary leave of absence and would be connected with the integrity commissioner.
The mover argued that an application process would not let Kitchener voters have a say, and that the gap to the next candidate after the fifth was much larger, so the fifth-place choice was clear.
